title: Migration in world history: the great movements of people since 1846
examples: What were the biggest migrations in modern history?

items.label: Europe → Americas
items.ask: What were the biggest migrations in modern history?

explain.say: We often picture migration as ships crossing the Atlantic to New York. But look at the sizes, from the historian Adam McKeown. Between 1846 and 1940 about 56 million people went from Europe to the Americas, about 50 million from India and southern China to South-East Asia, and about 48 million from Russia and China into northern Asia. Three huge streams, not one.

draw.text: Migration in world history: the great movements of people since 1846

items.label: Europe → Americas
items.ask: What were the biggest migrations in modern history?

explain.say: Look at the map. Ships left Liverpool for New York and Buenos Aires. Workers from Kolkata sailed as far as Fiji. Labourers from Guangzhou went to Singapore and the tin mines and plantations around it. Migrants built railways, cities and farms on every continent. Which of these routes had you heard of before?

Why move? See the causes. Push factors like Ireland's famine, when about a million died and a million left, and persecution, like pogroms against Jews in Russia. Pull factors like jobs and land. Steamships made travel cheaper, and letters and tickets from relatives pulled family members after them, called chain migration. Which cause is still strong today?

draw.name: x-why
draw.question: Why did so many people move after 1846?
draw.answer: Push, pull and the means to move all together.

explain.say: Movement was not always free. After slavery ended, over a million Indians went abroad as indentured labourers, bound to work for years on plantations. Then walls went up: America's Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and quota laws of 1924. After the Second World War came Partition and the 1951 Refugee Convention. See the timeline. Why do borders tighten in some decades?

explain.say: Now the historians. Oscar Handlin described migrants as uprooted and lonely; John Bodnar showed them transplanted, keeping families and cultures. McKeown widened the view beyond the Atlantic. Wonderful work. Challenge: trace one migration in your own family or town.

draw.verdict: Today: global, with migrants' own choices central.

faq.q: What were the biggest migrations in modern history?
faq.a: Adam McKeown estimated that between 1846 and 1940 about 55 to 58 million people moved from Europe to the Americas, 48 to 52 million from India and southern China to South-East Asia and the Indian Ocean, and 46 to 51 million from Russia and north-east Asia into Manchuria, Siberia and Central Asia.

Historians speak of push factors such as poverty, famine, war and persecution, pull factors such as jobs, land and safety, the means to travel, and networks of family and friends who help others follow, called chain migration.
asks: What are push and pull factors?

faq.a: A system in which workers signed contracts binding them to work for several years, often on plantations, in return for passage and wages. After slavery's abolition, over a million Indians, and many Chinese, went to places such as Mauritius, Trinidad, Guyana, Fiji and South Africa this way, often in harsh conditions.

faq.q: What was the Chinese Exclusion Act?
faq.a: A US law of 1882 that banned Chinese labourers from immigrating. It was the first major US law to exclude a group by nationality, and it was not repealed until 1943.
asks: When did the USA restrict immigration?

faq.a: A UN treaty of 1951 defining a refugee as someone with a well-founded fear of persecution, and forbidding states from sending refugees back to danger. A 1967 protocol extended it worldwide.

facts: Adam McKeown estimated about 55 to 58 million Europeans migrated to the Americas between 1846 and 1940.
The US Chinese Exclusion Act was passed in 1882.
The UN Refugee Convention was adopted in 1951.

quiz.say: Add McKeown's three streams: about 56, 50 and 48 million. About how many people is that?
quiz.why: 56 plus 50 plus 48 equals 154 million, about 150 million.

wrong.1: 56 million is only the European stream.
wrong.2: A billion is far more than these migrations.
